title: Lesson 17 - A3.1-A3.2 Legislation Overview
subject: Information Technology
bigQuestion: How does the law protect our data and computer systems?

sections.heading: Flying start (warm-up)
sections.text: Retrieval from A2, then think ahead. Try each one before reading the answer.
points: 1. What is meant by due diligence? Taking reasonable care and checks before trusting something, e.g. checking a supplier's security or getting an independent review
2. Which certification is needed to handle payment card data? PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard)
3. Name the three passive risk management measures. Risk acceptance, risk avoidance and risk transfer (check against your A2 notes)
4. Why must a penetration test always be authorised? Without permission, testing someone's system is unauthorised access, which is a crime
5. Two examples of personal data your school holds about you? E.g. your name, home address, date of birth, photo or medical notes
Think ahead: someone who breaks into a computer system that isn't theirs is committing a crime under the Computer Misuse Act 1990
Today's focus: why we need cyber security laws, UK GDPR (A3.1.1), the Computer Misuse Act 1990 (A3.1.2) and the four areas the laws apply to (A3.2.1–A3.2.4). Next: A3.3 legal responsibilities

sections.heading: Personally identifying information (PII)
sections.text: PII is any information that can identify a living person, on its own or combined with other information. UK GDPR says organisations must protect PII and justify every use of it.
points: Examples: name, home address, email, phone number, National Insurance number, bank details, photos, biometric data, IP address
Why is name + date of birth + postcode more dangerous together than alone? Together they can be used to steal someone's identity

sections.heading: Why do we need cyber security laws?
points: Computers and data run banking, healthcare, shopping and government
Without rules, little stops organisations misusing personal data
Laws set duties for organisations and rights for individuals
Courts can act, and every organisation meets the same standard
Think: should a global tech firm and a small local shop follow the same laws? The same standard protects everyone, but a small shop has far less money, staff and expertise to meet it

sections.heading: UK GDPR (A3.1.1)
sections.text: UK GDPR is the UK's main law on how personal data is collected, stored, used and shared, whether on paper, on a server or in the cloud. It is enforced by the ICO, with fines up to £17.5m or 4% of global turnover. The Data Protection Act 2018 works alongside it.

head: Duties on organisations
Rights of individuals
rows: See the data held about them
Keep it no longer than needed
Have data deleted when it's no longer needed
Justify every use of the data

points: Duty = what the ORGANISATION must do. Right = what the PERSON can ask for

sections.heading: Computer Misuse Act 1990 (A3.1.2)
sections.text: The CMA is the main UK law on unauthorised access to computers and data. A crime can happen even if nothing is stolen or damaged. The four offences match sections 1, 2, 3 and 3A of the Act.

head: Offence
What it means
rows: Getting into a system or data without permission
Getting in to commit a further crime, e.g. fraud
Changing, deleting or corrupting data without permission
Making, supplying or obtaining hacking software

sections.heading: The four areas the laws apply to (A3.2)
points: Mainly UK GDPR: Area 1, protecting data in storage and when transferred
Mainly UK GDPR: Area 2, privacy and PII (personally identifying information)
Mainly the CMA: Area 3, unauthorised access to computers and devices
Mainly the CMA: Area 4, access to and modification of data without permission
A serious incident often touches several areas at once

diagram.alt: Top: the four areas cyber security laws apply to. Mainly UK GDPR: 1, protecting data in storage and when transferred; 2, privacy and personally identifying information (PII). Mainly the Computer Misuse Act: 3, unauthorised access to computers and devices; 4, access to and modification of data without permission. Bottom: one incident, two laws. A hacker breaks into a hospital's patient database, which was never encrypted, and copies records. The hacker has committed Computer Misuse Act offences. The hospital may be investigated by the ICO under UK GDPR for not protecting the data.
diagram.caption: One incident can touch several areas, and both laws.

sections.heading: Areas 1 and 2: protecting data and PII
sections.text: Area 1 (storage and transfer): UK GDPR requires appropriate technical and organisational measures.
points: Storage: encrypt databases
Transfer: use HTTPS or a VPN
Area 2 (privacy and PII): organisations must justify every use of the PII they hold

sections.heading: Areas 3 and 4: unauthorised access and change
points: Area 3 (access to computers and devices): logging in to someone else's account or a server is a crime, even if no data is taken
Having your own login doesn't mean you can access everything
Area 4 (access to and modification of data): changing, deleting or planting data, e.g. altering exam results or installing ransomware
Area 4 may also breach UK GDPR if PII is involved

sections.heading: Case study: how the two laws work together
sections.text: A hacker breaks into a hospital's patient database from outside. They copy thousands of confidential patient records. The database had never been encrypted. Two different parties could face consequences.

head: UK GDPR
Computer Misuse Act 1990
rows: How data is protected and used
The hospital may be investigated by the ICO for not encrypting
The hacker has committed CMA offences

points: Ransomware: the attacker breaks the CMA; the organisation may breach UK GDPR if it didn't protect the data

sections.heading: Plenary: UK GDPR, Computer Misuse Act, or both?

Law
Why

Failing to protect data in storage
An employee logs in to a colleague's account to read their emails
A hacker breaks in and deletes thousands of customer records

points: Command words: Identify = pick from the information. Explain = point + linked reason. Describe = give an account

keyIdea: UK GDPR controls how organisations protect and use personal data (duties for organisations, rights for individuals, enforced by the ICO). The Computer Misuse Act 1990 makes unauthorised access, access with intent, modification and hacking tools crimes for individuals. One incident can involve both: the attacker breaks the CMA, and the organisation may breach UK GDPR if it didn't protect the data.

The UK law that works alongside UK GDPR
ICO
The Information Commissioner's Office: enforces UK GDPR, with fines up to £17.5m or 4% of global turnover
GDPR duties on organisations
Keep personal data secure, only collect what is needed, keep it no longer than needed, justify every use of it
GDPR rights of individuals
See the data held about them, have wrong data corrected, have data deleted when it's no longer needed
Computer Misuse Act 1990 (CMA)
The main UK law on unauthorised access to computers and data. A crime can happen even if nothing is stolen or damaged
CMA: unauthorised access
Getting into a system or data without permission
CMA: access with intent
Getting in to commit a further crime, e.g. fraud
CMA: modification
Changing, deleting or corrupting data without permission
CMA: hacking tools
Making, supplying or obtaining hacking software
Area 1: protecting data
Data in storage and when transferred (mainly UK GDPR), e.g. encrypt databases, use HTTPS or a VPN
Area 2: privacy and PII
Organisations must justify every use of the PII they hold (mainly UK GDPR)
Area 3: unauthorised access
Accessing computers and devices without permission (mainly CMA). A crime even if no data is taken
Area 4: access and modification
Changing, deleting or planting data without permission, e.g. altering exam results or installing ransomware (mainly CMA)
Technical and organisational measures
What UK GDPR requires to protect data, e.g. encryption, secure connections and clear procedures
Who each law targets
UK GDPR: organisations that hold personal data. CMA: individuals who misuse systems
Ransomware and the law
The attacker breaks the CMA; the organisation may breach UK GDPR if it didn't protect the data

o: Any data stored on a computer
Any information that can identify a living person, alone or combined with other information
quiz.e: PII is personally identifying information about a living person, on its own or combined.

quiz.q: Why is name + date of birth + postcode more dangerous together than alone?
o: Together they can be used to steal someone's identity
quiz.e: Combined, they're enough to impersonate someone.
The Information Commissioner's Office enforces UK GDPR.

quiz.q: What is the maximum UK GDPR fine?
quiz.e: Up to £17.5m or 4% of global turnover.

quiz.q: Which of these is a RIGHT of individuals under UK GDPR, not a duty on organisations?
o: Justify every use of the data
quiz.e: Having data corrected is something a person can ask for. The others are duties.

quiz.q: Which of these is a DUTY on organisations under UK GDPR?
o: Keep data no longer than needed
See the data held about you
quiz.e: Not keeping data too long is a duty. The others are individuals' rights.

quiz.q: Under the CMA, can it be a crime to get into a system even if nothing is stolen or damaged?
o: No, only if data is stolen
No, only if data is damaged
Yes, unauthorised access alone is a crime
Only if the system belongs to the government
quiz.e: Getting in without permission is an offence on its own.

quiz.q: Someone gets into a bank's system to commit fraud. Which CMA offence?
quiz.e: Getting in to commit a further crime, like fraud, is access with intent.

quiz.q: Someone changes a student's exam results without permission. Which CMA offence?
quiz.e: Changing data without permission is modification.

quiz.q: A student downloads a password-cracking tool. Which law is involved?
quiz.e: Obtaining hacking tools is a CMA offence.

quiz.q: Which two areas does UK GDPR mainly apply to?
o: Protecting data (storage and transfer) and privacy and PII
quiz.e: Areas 1 and 2 are mainly UK GDPR; areas 3 and 4 are mainly the CMA.

quiz.q: How should data be protected while it is being transferred?
o: Store it on a USB stick
quiz.e: HTTPS or a VPN encrypts it, so it can't be read if intercepted.

quiz.q: An employee has their own login. Does that mean they can access everything?
o: Yes, any login gives full access
No, accessing areas they're not permitted to use is still unauthorised
quiz.e: Having your own login doesn't mean you can access everything.

quiz.q: In the hospital breach, which law applies to the HOSPITAL that never encrypted its database?
o: UK GDPR (it may be investigated by the ICO)
quiz.e: The hospital failed to protect data in storage, so it may be investigated under UK GDPR.

quiz.q: Who does the Computer Misuse Act mainly target?
quiz.e: The CMA targets individuals who misuse systems; UK GDPR targets organisations holding personal data.

apply.title: UK GDPR, Computer Misuse Act, or both?
apply.intro: Decide which law applies to each scenario. Think about who did what: an organisation handling data (GDPR) or a person misusing a system (CMA).

items.task: A hospital stores patient records in an unencrypted database.
items.e: Failing to protect data in storage: UK GDPR.

items.task: An employee logs in to a colleague's account to read their emails.
A hacker breaks in and deletes thousands of customer records that were poorly protected.
items.e: Hacker: CMA. Company: GDPR, because the data was poorly protected.

items.task: A website keeps customers' passport numbers for years with no reason.
items.e: Keeping data longer than needed: UK GDPR.

items.task: A student downloads a password-cracking tool.
A shop collects customers' National Insurance numbers just to send a receipt.
items.e: Collecting more than is needed: UK GDPR.

items.task: A student logs in to the school system with a teacher's password and changes their own grades.
Ransomware encrypts a company's customer database, which had no backups or security updates.
items.e: Attacker: CMA. Company: may breach UK GDPR for not protecting the data.

items.task: A company sends customer records to a partner over plain, unencrypted email. Which area is this?
o: Area 1: protecting data in storage and transfer
items.e: Data in transfer isn't protected. It should use HTTPS or a VPN.

items.task: Someone sells hacking software online. Which CMA offence?
items.e: Making, supplying or obtaining hacking software.

exam.sc: Oakridge Dental stores patients' names, addresses, dates of birth and medical notes. It sends records to a hospital.
exam.q: 1. Identify three items of PII that Oakridge holds.
pts: Names
Addresses
Dates of birth / medical notes (any three, 1 mark each)
exam.tip: "Identify" = pick from the information given. Don't add items that aren't in the scenario.

exam.sc: Oakridge Dental stores patients' names, addresses, dates of birth and medical notes. It sends records to a hospital.
exam.q: 2. Explain one way Oakridge could protect patient data while it is sent to the hospital.
pts: A method, e.g. encrypt the data or use a secure connection (HTTPS/VPN)
Why: if it is intercepted it can't be read
exam.tip: Method + linked reason. Make sure it's about data being SENT, not stored.

exam.q: 3. Describe the purpose of the Computer Misuse Act 1990.
pts: Makes it a crime to access computers or data without permission
Makes it a crime to change or delete data without permission
Makes it a crime to make or supply hacking tools
exam.tip: Give an account of three different things it makes illegal.

exam.q: 4. Explain why one ransomware attack could involve both UK GDPR and the Computer Misuse Act.
pts: The attacker breaks the CMA by accessing and modifying data without permission
The organisation may breach UK GDPR if it didn't protect the data
exam.tip: Name each party and the law that applies to them.

exam.q: 5. Explain why a person's name, date of birth and postcode are more dangerous together than alone.
pts: Together they can identify one specific person
so they can be used to steal that person's identity
exam.tip: Link the combination to identity theft.

exam.q: 6. State one duty UK GDPR places on organisations and one right it gives individuals.
pts: Duty, e.g. keep personal data secure / only collect what is needed / keep it no longer than needed / justify every use
Right, e.g. see the data held about them / have wrong data corrected / have it deleted
exam.tip: A duty is what the organisation must do; a right is what the person can ask for.

exam.sc: A hacker breaks into a hospital's patient database from outside and copies thousands of confidential patient records. The database had never been encrypted.
exam.q: 7. Explain which law applies to each party in this incident.
pts: The hacker has broken the Computer Misuse Act
because they accessed the database and copied records without permission
The hospital may be investigated by the ICO under UK GDPR
because it never encrypted the database, so it failed to keep personal data secure
exam.tip: Two parties, two laws: give each one a point and a linked reason from the scenario.

exam.q: 8. Explain why cyber security laws are needed.
pts: Computers and data run banking, healthcare, shopping and government / without rules little stops organisations misusing data
so laws set duties and rights that courts can enforce, and every organisation meets the same standard
exam.tip: Give the problem, then what the law does about it.

exam.sc: Jordan works in a company's sales team and has their own login. They use it to open the HR folder and read colleagues' salary details, which they are not allowed to see.
exam.q: 9. Explain whether Jordan has committed an offence.
pts: Yes, unauthorised access under the Computer Misuse Act
because having their own login doesn't give permission to access the HR data, even if nothing is changed or taken
exam.tip: Remember: a crime can happen even if nothing is stolen or damaged.
